title: LCA of Cocoa Production and Chocolate: From Farm to Wrapper
sub: A cradle-to-grave assessment of a milk chocolate bar, with a comparison of conventional, certified deforestation-free and agroforestry cocoa.
pdf: Case 01 — LCA of Cocoa Production and Chocolate: Executive Summary
fu: One 100 g milk chocolate bar (30% cocoa solids) purchased and eaten in Germany
ref: 105 g of chocolate produced (100 g eaten + 5 g wasted along retail and household), made from 36 g cocoa beans, 46 g sugar and 28 g milk powder, packed in a 4 g paper sleeve and 2 g aluminium-PE inner foil
boundary: Cradle-to-grave: farm inputs and land-use change, post-harvest, ingredients, manufacturing, packaging, distribution, retail, consumption and disposal of packaging and wasted product
geo: Cocoa from Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana; milk powder and beet sugar from the EU; manufacturing, retail and consumption in Germany
time: Technology and practices of 2024–2026; GWP100 (IPCC AR6); land-use change emissions amortised over 20 years
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100 for climate change; AWARE for water scarcity; ReCiPe 2016 land occupation
alloc: Cocoa butter, liquor and shells allocated by economic value; milk to milk powder by dry-matter content; packaging recycling via cut-off approach
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (e.g., emulsifier lecithin, vanilla, printing inks) provided cumulative exclusions <5%
dq: Secondary data from public LCA studies and databases; land-use change from sourcing-region averages; no farm-level primary data. Overall data quality: Medium, Low for land-use change
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges reported by Poore & Nemecek (2018), Konstantas et al. (2018), Agribalyse and ecoinvent cocoa datasets.
loop: Circular loop: paper sleeve recycled; cocoa shells used as feed, fuel or mulch
exec:
This case study assesses a 100 g milk chocolate bar from cocoa farm to wrapper disposal. Chocolate matters because cocoa is a high-risk commodity under the EU Deforestation Regulation, its supply chain involves around five to six million smallholder farmers, and its footprint is dominated by agriculture rather than factories.
The illustrative baseline result is 1.25 kg CO2e per bar. Cocoa cultivation, including land-use change, contributes about 45%, and milk powder and sugar a further 30%. Manufacturing, packaging, distribution and end-of-life together account for less than a quarter. Cocoa farming also dominates water consumption, land use and biodiversity pressure.
Sourcing deforestation-free cocoa reduces climate impact by about 30% in this model, and agroforestry cocoa by about 37%, although agroforestry needs slightly more land per tonne. A combined pathway with renewable energy at the factory and less product waste reaches about 45% lower emissions.
The key recommendation is to prioritise traceable, deforestation-free sourcing and supplier programmes before investing in packaging changes, which have a small effect on totals. For CSRD reporting, the findings are most relevant to ESRS E1 (Scope 3 Category 1), E4 (biodiversity and land-use change) and S2 (workers in the value chain, including child-labour risk).
overview:
Milk chocolate is made from cocoa liquor and cocoa butter combined with sugar and milk powder, then refined, conched, tempered and moulded. Most cocoa is grown by smallholders in West Africa, fermented and sun-dried on farms, and shipped as beans to processors in Europe.
The purpose of this LCA is to identify where a chocolate brand's environmental impacts arise, how much sourcing choices change them, and which results can support supply-chain decarbonisation targets, EUDR due diligence and CSRD reporting.
goal: The goal is to support a chocolate brand's sourcing and decarbonisation strategy by quantifying the life-cycle impacts of a typical milk chocolate bar and comparing three cocoa sourcing models. The intended audience is procurement, sustainability and ESG reporting teams. Results are for internal decision-making and are not intended for comparative public claims.

stages.what: Cocoa trees are grown on smallholder farms; pods are harvested by hand and beans removed.
stages.in: Land, fertiliser (N, P, K), pesticides, seedlings, labour
stages.out: Wet cocoa beans, pod husks (left on farm)
stages.ew: Mostly rain-fed; limited irrigation; manual operations
stages.em: N2O from fertiliser; CO2 from land-use change where forest is cleared
stages.tr: Farm to local collection point by foot, motorbike or truck
stages.so: Low farmer incomes, child-labour risk, deforestation in protected areas
stages.as: Yield 500 kg/ha; 10% of cocoa from land converted within 20 years (illustrative)

stages.what: Beans are fermented in heaps, sun-dried, bagged and shipped to Europe.
stages.in: Wet beans, jute bags, diesel for trucks, heavy fuel oil for shipping
stages.ew: Sun drying; small amounts of diesel
stages.tr: 300 km truck to port; 7,000 km container ship to Amsterdam
stages.so: Price volatility, limited traceability between farm and cooperative
stages.as: Transport distances typical for Abidjan/Tema to Northern Europe

stages.what: Dairy farming and milk drying; sugar beet cultivation and refining in the EU.
stages.em: Methane from cattle, N2O from soils, CO2 from processing
stages.wa: Beet pulp (used as feed), dairy wastewater
stages.tr: Within the EU, average 500 km by truck
stages.as: EU average datasets; milk powder allocated by dry matter

stages.what: Roasting, winnowing, grinding, pressing, mixing, refining, conching, tempering and moulding.
stages.in: Dry beans, sugar, milk powder, electricity, natural gas, water
stages.ew: 0.35 kWh electricity and 0.6 MJ heat per bar
stages.em: CO2 from energy use; refrigerant leakage
stages.wa: Shells (sold as feed, mulch or fuel), production losses 3%
stages.as: German grid mix; natural gas heat

stages.what: Production of the paper sleeve and aluminium-PE inner foil.
stages.ew: Electricity and heat for paper and foil production
stages.as: 4 g paper (50% recycled), 2 g foil laminate

stages.what: Transport to distribution centres and supermarkets; storage at ambient temperature.
stages.ew: Store lighting and climate control allocated by shelf space
stages.em: CO2 from trucks and store energy
stages.as: Retail energy allocated by product volume

stages.what: Consumers eat the bar; packaging and wasted chocolate are disposed of.
stages.em: CO2 from incineration of foil-laminate and food waste
stages.wa: Paper sleeve (75% recycled), foil laminate incinerated

hot.why: Clearing forest for cocoa releases stored carbon and destroys habitat. Even with only 10% of supply from recently converted land, it contributes about 30% of the climate result, and it is the main biodiversity risk.
Dairy farming emits methane and nitrous oxide, and drying milk is energy-intensive. Milk powder is the largest single ingredient impact after cocoa.
Nitrogen fertiliser drives N2O emissions and freshwater eutrophication; pesticide use adds toxicity pressure. Practices vary widely between farms.

hot.t: Water and land occupation in producing regions
hot.why: Cocoa needs large areas of tropical land per kg of product, and irrigation in the dry season can occur in basins under seasonal stress.
Conching and refining run for hours; electricity and gas are the main controllable Scope 1 and 2 sources for a chocolate maker.

desc: Average West African sourcing, 10% from recently deforested land
Traceable, verified deforestation-free supply (no land-use change); same farm practices
Deforestation-free cocoa grown under shade trees with 40% less synthetic fertiliser; lower yield per hectare; tree carbon removals not credited
Agroforestry cocoa plus renewable electricity and heat at the factory, paper-only wrapper and 50% less product waste

sens.t: Sensitivity: share of cocoa from recently deforested land
sens.xl: Share of cocoa from land converted in the last 20 years (%)
sens.note: Land-use change is the most uncertain and most influential parameter. Each 5 percentage points of supply from recently converted land adds about 0.19 kg CO2e per bar.
sens.interp: The result more than doubles between fully deforestation-free supply and a 25% share from converted land. Traceability to farm level is therefore worth more than refinements in any other part of the model.

ci.stage: Cocoa cultivation is the largest stage because of land-use change and fertiliser; milk powder and sugar follow. Stages under the manufacturer's direct control (factory, packaging) make up about 12% of the total.
ci.stage_e: Energy demand is spread more evenly: milk drying and factory processes dominate, as cocoa farming uses little machinery.
ci.stage_w: Water consumption is concentrated at farm level, so water risk depends on where cocoa and milk are produced.
ci.donut: About three quarters of the climate result occurs before ingredients reach the factory, so most reductions require supplier engagement (Scope 3).
ci.sankey: Only about a third of the bar's mass is cocoa; sugar and milk powder make up the rest. Cocoa shells leave the system as a co-product rather than waste.
ci.heat: Cultivation is a hotspot across climate, water, land and eutrophication; manufacturing is a hotspot only for energy.
ci.scen: Removing land-use change is the single largest lever. Factory and packaging measures add smaller, but fully controllable, reductions.
ci.radar: Agroforestry lowers climate, water and eutrophication but increases land occupation, a trade-off that should be reported alongside biodiversity benefits that LCA does not fully capture.
ci.wf: Around 80% of the achievable reduction in this pathway comes from sourcing decisions rather than operations.

interp.m: The climate footprint of chocolate is driven by agriculture. Sourcing decisions determine most of the result, and land-use change can make the difference between a moderate and a high footprint.
interp.a: The share of cocoa from recently converted land; the amortisation period for land-use change (20 years); cocoa yield per hectare; the milk content of the recipe; allocation between cocoa butter and cocoa powder.
interp.u: Land-use change data are regional averages with high uncertainty. Farm practices vary widely. Agroforestry carbon removals are excluded because permanence and measurement are uncertain.
interp.can: Cocoa sourcing and milk powder are the main hotspots. Deforestation-free sourcing reduces climate impact substantially. Packaging changes have a small effect on the total.
interp.cannot: The study cannot determine the footprint of a specific supplier, certify a product as deforestation-free, or support public comparative claims. It does not quantify biodiversity loss or farmer income effects.
interp.d: Prioritising traceable sourcing programmes; setting Scope 3 reduction targets for cocoa and dairy; deciding on supplier engagement and premiums; focusing packaging work on recyclability rather than carbon.

recs: Explore recipes with lower milk content or alternative dairy sources, and design paper-only mono-material wrappers that maintain shelf life.
Make farm-level traceability (geolocation polygons) and deforestation-free verification contract requirements; reward agroforestry practices through premiums.
Switch to renewable electricity, electrify or recover heat in roasting and conching, and valorise cocoa shells.
Reduce retail losses through demand forecasting and markdowns; avoid unsubstantiated 'climate-neutral' claims.
Support collection of paper sleeves and composite foils; process food waste through anaerobic digestion.
Use the LCA to set Scope 3 targets by ingredient, report land-use change emissions separately, and link EUDR due diligence data to ESRS E4 metrics.
Support smallholder traceability systems and living-income programmes so that EUDR compliance does not exclude small farmers.
csrd: Relevant ESRS topics
E1 Climate change; E3 Water; E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems; E5 Resource use (packaging); S2 Workers in the value chain; S3 Affected communities; G1 Business conduct
Relevant disclosure requirements
E1-6 gross Scope 1, 2, 3 emissions; E1-4 targets; E1-1 transition plan; E4 impact metrics on land-use change; S2 policies and actions on value-chain workers (Set 1 numbering)
Material impacts
Deforestation and biodiversity loss in cocoa regions; agricultural GHG emissions; child labour and low incomes in the value chain
Material risks
EUDR non-compliance (market access); supply disruption from climate change in West Africa; reputational risk
Material opportunities
Premium for traceable cocoa; resilient supply through agroforestry; lower Scope 3 through sourcing
Value-chain relevance
About 80% of the climate result is upstream (cocoa, dairy, sugar); disclosures depend on supplier data
Scope 1, 2 and 3
Scope 1: factory gas (~3%). Scope 2: factory electricity (~6%). Scope 3: Cat. 1 purchased goods (~80%), Cat. 4 and 9 transport, Cat. 12 end-of-life
Climate transition risks
Carbon pricing on dairy and energy; customer requirements for low-carbon products; EUDR traceability costs
Physical climate risks
Heat and drought stress reduce cocoa yields; shifting suitable growing areas in West Africa
Circular-economy indicators
Packaging recycled content and recyclability; cocoa shell valorisation rate; food waste
Pollution indicators
Fertiliser and pesticide use; freshwater eutrophication
Water indicators
Water consumption and AWARE scarcity in sourcing regions
Biodiversity indicators
Land use and land-use change (ha), share of deforestation-free volume, share sourced near protected areas
Social risks
Child labour, farmer living income, land rights; requires human-rights due diligence beyond LCA
Governance & internal controls
Documented LCA method; supplier data validation; reconciliation of LCA-based Scope 3 with purchased volumes; review by internal audit

lim: Farm-level fertiliser use, yields and land-use history; cooperative-level transport; actual retail energy
West African averages; Latin American or Asian cocoa would differ, particularly for land-use change
Economic allocation between butter, liquor and shells; mass allocation would shift burden to shells
High for land-use change (±50% or more); medium for dairy and manufacturing
Supplier and cooperative data, polygon-level traceability, factory energy metering, actual recipe and packaging specifications
take: For chocolate, the farm matters more than the factory: verified deforestation-free and agroforestry cocoa can cut the bar's climate footprint by roughly a third, far more than any packaging change.
biz: Make traceable, deforestation-free cocoa the core of the decarbonisation and EUDR programme, set ingredient-level Scope 3 targets for cocoa and dairy, and treat packaging work as a recyclability rather than a carbon priority.
assume: 10% of cocoa from land converted within 20 years; 20-year amortisation of land-use change; agroforestry tree carbon not credited; economic allocation of cocoa co-products; German grid mix; 5% product waste. Biodiversity and social impacts are discussed qualitatively only.
